title: Joel Theatrical Rigging v. The Queen (2016 TCC 162)
subject: TCC appeal examining routine engineering, hypothesis formulation, and documentation in theatrical rigging design.
outcome: Appeal dismissed; court held custom rigging design without testable hypotheses or scientific method was routine engineering.
summary: Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 6) is a Tax Court of Canada informal-procedure decision denying an Ontario rigging contractor's SR&ED claims for its 2008 and 2009 taxation years. For Canadian businesses claiming SR&ED, the key takeaway is that unmeasured trial-and-error testing without testable hypotheses or contemporaneous records will not qualify.
metaDescription: Analyze the 2016 TCC 162 SR&ED ruling for Joel Theatrical Rigging (JTR) Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen in the Tax Court of Canada.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary and Case Background

The decision of the Tax Court of Canada in Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen (Docket 2015-125(IT)I, heard under the Informal Procedure at Toronto on July 4, 2016 and rendered by Justice Don R. Sommerfeldt on January 17, 2017, neutral citation 2017 TCC 6) is a frequently cited decision in Canadian Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) jurisprudence, although, having been rendered under the Informal Procedure, it is not to be treated as a precedent for other cases (section 18.28 of the Tax Court of Canada Act). The ruling addresses the persistent tension between practical shop-floor mechanical problem-solving and the strict statutory standard of a "systematic investigation or search" carried out by means of experiment or analysis under subsection 248(1) of the Canadian Income Tax Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "Act"). For Canadian corporate taxpayers, engineering contractors, and tax advisors, Justice Sommerfeldt's reasons illustrate how the Court applies the judicial definition of a hypothesis ("a statement to be tested by an experiment or a trial") and why unmeasured, iterative mechanical testing may be characterized as trial and error or routine engineering rather than as a systematic investigation.
Factual Matrix and the Taxpayer's Claim

The Appellant, Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. ("JTR"), is an Ontario-based corporation headquartered in Mississauga and established in 1980. JTR specializes in the custom design, manufacture, and installation of theatrical and television rigging systems, pipe and wire-way grids, counterweight rigging, motorized house curtains, and emergency fire curtain assemblies for performing arts venues, arenas, and television studios. During the relevant taxation periods, the corporation operated under the direction of its president and owner, Mr. Van Marineau, who had worked at JTR for 36 years, beginning as an equipment installer; the decision does not establish when he acquired the business (counsel's statement that he purchased it in 1966 was considered unlikely by the Court, which held that nothing turned on the date of purchase).

For its taxation years ending April 30, 2008 and April 30, 2009, JTR submitted two SR&ED claims on Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) seeking current expenditure deductions under subsection 37(1) of the Act and refundable Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) under subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the Act. In its technical narratives, JTR stated that it sought to advance technology in the field of applied mechanics—specifically theatrical rigging equipment—by undertaking experimental development aimed at solving two distinct mechanical problems encountered in its commercial operations.

The first of the two projects examined at trial was the "Fire Curtain Project" (2008 taxation year; June 2007 to April 2008), which focused on developing a system using only a motor, a hydraulic pump, valves and related equipment, without counterweights, capable of controlling the rate of descent of the fire curtain in a theatre at Ryerson University and subsequently the fire curtains at the Richmond Hill Theatre and the Persephone Theatre in Saskatoon. Until then, JTR and other participants in the theatrical rigging business had used counterweights to control the rate of descent, but counterweights occupied additional space and created a larger footprint in the theatre; JTR's claim also noted that fire curtains, historically made of heavy asbestos, were now made of a new lightweight material called Zetex. The applicable fire code regulations required a fire curtain to descend in 30 seconds or less, while too fast a descent risked injuring someone caught below the curtain or causing fear or panic in the audience, and JTR found that the backwind system on a standard motor was not capable of producing a slow, controlled descent. JTR experimented in its shop by hoisting a weight of approximately 800 pounds (an estimate of the weight of the Ryerson University fire curtain), releasing the motor's brake and watching the weight fall, while adding hydraulic pumps, hoses and valves in various arrangements, and ultimately developed a system able to achieve a controlled descent for 95% of all fire curtains. JTR asserted that the development of this system, together with its second project (the "Manual Override Project" of its 2009 taxation year, carried out from May to September 2008, which developed a hand-crank system allowing the curtain cable drum to be disengaged and operated manually during a power failure or machine malfunction without disorienting the limit switch), required overcoming technological uncertainties that went beyond standard rigging practices.
The Tax Authority's Challenge

Following a technical and financial review, the Minister of National Revenue (the "Minister"), acting through the Canada Revenue Agency (the "CRA"), issued Notices of Reassessment on March 15, 2011 and January 6, 2012, disallowing JTR's claimed SR&ED expenditures and associated ITCs in their entirety. The CRA's denial rested on the determination that JTR's activities did not constitute SR&ED as defined in subsection 248(1) of the Act because they did not satisfy the five requirements outlined in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants.

In defending the reassessments before the Tax Court, the Crown maintained a series of interlocking legal and technical objections. First, the Minister argued that the mechanical challenges encountered by JTR did not involve genuine "technological risk or uncertainty" that could not be resolved through routine engineering, standard mechanical design calculations, or established rigging procedures. Second, the Crown contended that JTR failed to formulate specific, testable scientific or technological hypotheses aimed at reducing or eliminating an identified uncertainty prior to conducting its physical trials. Third, the Minister assumed that systematic investigation or research was not performed as part of the Fire Curtain Project; the absence of basic quantitative measurements (the exact test weight was never determined and the duration of each descent was never timed) emerged from Mr. Marineau's testimony at trial and was relied on by the Court. Fourth, the evidence showed that JTR kept no contemporaneous notes, sketches, drawings or records of changes in variables and results for either project, and the Experiment Summary Sheets produced at trial were prepared by JTR's advisor, Sheldon & Milstein Tax Consultants Ltd., after the experiments had been completed. The Minister also assumed that the claimed 2008 activities were limited to the design, purchasing, adjustments, arrangements, pump selection and valve changes relating to three customer contracts (Ryerson University, the Richmond Hill Theatre and the Persephone Theatre) and constituted routine work for JTR, and the Court found that JTR had not discharged its burden of disproving these assumptions.
Governing Statutory and Jurisprudential Framework

In Canadian income tax law, the availability of SR&ED tax incentives is governed by an integrated statutory regime under the Income Tax Act and the Income Tax Regulations. Subsection 37(1) permits a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada to deduct qualified current SR&ED expenditures incurred in the year into an expenditure pool that may be deducted currently or carried forward indefinitely, while subsections 127(5) and 127(9) provide Investment Tax Credits—including a basic non-refundable ITC for general corporations (currently 15%, and 20% for the 2008 and 2009 taxation years at issue) and an enhanced refundable ITC for Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) up to their expenditure limit—provided the taxpayer files the prescribed Form T661 containing prescribed information within 12 months of its corporate income tax filing due date pursuant to subsection 37(11) and, to claim ITCs, files the prescribed form (Schedule 31) within the same period pursuant to paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9).

The substantive gateway to these incentives is the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Act, which defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". For industrial and commercial taxpayers, eligibility typically hinges on paragraph (c) of subsection 248(1) ("experimental development"), which encompasses work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Simultaneously, subsection 248(1) expressly excludes from SR&ED activities such as routine data collection, quality control, routine testing, style changes, market research, and the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product.

Because the statutory text of subsection 248(1) is concise, Canadian courts evaluate scientific eligibility through the binding five-question jurisprudential framework formulated by Justice Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC), [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, and affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. Canada, 1998 CanLII 8876 (FCA) and CW Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393. Under this five-part judicial test, the Court first asks whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. If such an uncertainty existed, the Court second asks whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. Third, the Court evaluates whether the procedures adopted accorded with established and objective principles of the scientific method, characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement, and experiment, and the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses. Fourth, the Court determines whether the process resulted in a technological advancement. Fifth, the Court examines whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the results was kept as the work progressed, noting that while the Income Tax Act and the Income Tax Regulations do not expressly mandate written records as a statutory precondition, contemporaneous documentation is vital to discharging the evidentiary burden.
The Court's Final Holding

Justice Sommerfeldt dismissed JTR's appeals from the reassessments of its 2008 and 2009 taxation years, without costs. Applying the Northwest Hydraulic framework to the testimonial and documentary evidence adduced at trial—consisting of the testimony of JTR's president, Mr. Van Marineau, and Mr. Todd Louie, an accountant and Director of Taxation at Sheldon & Milstein Tax Consultants Ltd., the advisor that prepared the claims (no scientist, engineer or expert witness testified, and the Respondent called no witnesses)—the Tax Court concluded that JTR failed to establish on a balance of probabilities that its 2008 and 2009 rigging projects constituted SR&ED.

Justice Sommerfeldt stated that the work done on the Fire Curtain Project "may well have been routine engineering" rather than a response to a true technological uncertainty, and found that the technological uncertainty in the Manual Override Project had not been clearly articulated and that its work was routine engineering. In addition, the purported hypotheses in the Experiment Summary Sheets were not formulated as propositions or suppositions to be tested (a hypothesis being "a statement to be tested by an experiment or a trial"); while certain hypotheses stated in Part 2 of the claims may have qualified, the steps they contemplated appeared to be routine engineering, and the experimentation was characterized as trial and error rather than the scientific method. Because Mr. Marineau and his team did not determine the precise weight of the approximately 800-pound test weight used in their trials and did not measure the duration of the descents from one trial to the next, the Court found that the Fire Curtain experiments appeared to be trial and error rather than systematic experimentation. Because no scientist or engineer testified, the Court had no reliable evidence of the general understanding of persons knowledgeable in mechanical engineering in 2007 through 2009, JTR's descriptions of its advancements read as statements of objectives rather than technological advancements, and JTR kept no contemporaneous records of its experiments.
2. Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures

A rigorous legal and technical dissection of Justice Sommerfeldt's decision in Joel Theatrical Rigging reveals five cascading deficiencies that proved fatal to the Appellant's claim. In Canadian tax litigation, the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria operate cumulatively; a failure on any one of the first four substantive elements disqualifies the project, while a failure on the fifth element (contemporaneous documentation) severely compromises the taxpayer's ability to discharge its evidentiary burden on the first four. In JTR, the deficiencies spanned every rung of this analytical ladder, providing a clear illustration of why shop-floor product development frequently fails under judicial scrutiny.
Failure to Differentiate Technological Uncertainty from Routine Engineering

The threshold inquiry in any SR&ED dispute is whether the taxpayer encountered a genuine "technological uncertainty" that could not be resolved by routine engineering or standard procedures. Justice Sommerfeldt reiterated the settled legal standard that to constitute SR&ED, a particular project must address a problem or type of uncertainty that cannot be resolved by applying established engineering principles, known formulas, or standard industry practices available to a competent professional in the field.

In JTR, the Appellant framed its challenge in terms of functional product performance: controlling the rate of descent of a fire curtain using only a motor, a hydraulic pump and valves, without counterweights, within the 30-second fire code limit and, as its claim noted, for lighter Zetex curtains of varying sizes; Mr. Marineau testified that at the outset he and his colleagues had no idea how to achieve this and that his online and patent research found nothing that would assist. However, in Canadian tax law, a commercial or functional design objective is not synonymous with a technological uncertainty. Under Northwest Hydraulic and its progeny, technological uncertainty arises either where it is uncertain whether a given objective can be achieved at all due to a fundamental gap in underlying scientific or engineering knowledge, or where "system uncertainty" exists—meaning that although individual components or physical laws are known (such as pulleys, counterweights, friction brakes, hydraulic dampers, and gravitational acceleration), their integration or interaction within a newly constrained system creates unpredictable conflicts that standard engineering calculations cannot model or resolve.

JTR failed to establish what techniques, procedures and data were generally accessible to competent mechanical engineers in 2008 and 2009, because no scientist or engineer testified; the four patents produced by Mr. Louie, an accountant who was not qualified as an expert and could not describe the search terms used to find them, did not persuade the Court that they represented the totality of available technology. Mr. Marineau acknowledged that the motors, gear boxes, pumps, valves and other equipment used were all standard products, and the Court found that the challenge of combining them to control the duration of the descent was resolved by routine engineering or standard procedures or, if not, constituted trial and error. Noting that JTR neither had a professional engineer on its team nor consulted one during the experiments (although its usual practice was to have installation plans reviewed and stamped by a professional engineer), and that JTR had not disproved the Minister's assumption that the work was routine, Justice Sommerfeldt was not persuaded that no available technology would have been found had a professional engineer been consulted, and concluded that the work on the Fire Curtain Project "may well have been routine engineering". Looking forward, this aspect of the ruling signals to Canadian engineering contractors that any SR&ED claim must begin by documenting the exact boundary of standard engineering practice and proving empirically why textbook methodologies failed.
Absence of Testable Hypotheses Preceding Experimental Trials

The second major failure in JTR—whose definition of a hypothesis has been cited in subsequent Tax Court decisions such as Dave's Diesel Inc. v. The Queen, 2022 TCC 62, and Vortex Energy Services Ltd. v. The King, 2025 TCC 63 (while Dock Edge + Inc. v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 11, cited JTR on the absence of engineering evidence regarding routine engineering)—lies in the inadequate formulation of hypotheses in the Appellant's records.

At paragraph 26 of the decision, relying on Advanced Agricultural Testing Inc. v. The Queen, 2009 TCC 190, Justice Sommerfeldt crystallized the legal definition of a hypothesis for SR&ED purposes: "...a hypothesis is a statement to be tested by an experiment or a trial." In applying this requirement, after reviewing dictionary and judicial definitions of the term (including those in Maritime-Ontario Freight Lines and C.W. Agencies), the Tax Court examined whether JTR's stated hypotheses were formulated as propositions or suppositions to be tested. Although the decision does not frame it in these terms, an overarching commercial goal—such as whether a rigging system could achieve a controlled descent for 95% of fire curtains—merely defines the desired business outcome. By contrast, an eligible testable hypothesis is a specific, predictive proposition formulated prior to an experiment that posits a causal relationship between an independent variable (such as the location of the hydraulic pump on the motor, the valve configuration, or hydraulic flow restriction) and a dependent variable (such as terminal descent velocity and deceleration profile for a specified curtain mass), which is then subjected to empirical verification or falsification.

As subsequent Tax Court jurisprudence applying JTR has emphasized, the Northwest Hydraulic criteria do not contemplate a single, overarching hypothesis for an entire commercial endeavour, but rather a series of particular, sequential hypotheses that precede each experimental iteration. In JTR, the purported hypotheses for the Fire Curtain Project appeared only in the "next steps" entries of Experiment Summary Sheets prepared by Sheldon after the experiments were completed, were not formulated as propositions or suppositions to be tested (for example, "Hypothesis is to experiment with hydraulic pumps and valves"), and were absent for Experiments 1, 5, 6 and 7, while for the Manual Override Project the same purported hypothesis was repeated for three successive experiments despite unsuccessful results. Instead, they modified mechanical configurations reactively until the falling test weight appeared, to the naked eye, to descend at a controlled speed. Without a pre-formulated proposition explaining why a specific mechanical modification was expected to alter the physical system in a predictable manner, the work could not satisfy the second Northwest Hydraulic criterion; the Court did accept that the Part 2 statement in the 2008 claim (that connecting the hydraulic pump to the rotor end rather than the gearing end of the motor would create sufficient oil pressure) may have been a hypothesis, and that the hypotheses described in Part 2 of the 2009 claim were adequately formulated, but held that the steps those hypotheses contemplated appeared to be routine engineering rather than SR&ED.
Lack of Systematic Investigation and Quantitative Measurement

A third central failure in JTR was the absence of a thorough experimental process conforming to the scientific method. Even where a taxpayer operates in an informal shop-floor environment rather than an academic or institutional laboratory, the third Northwest Hydraulic criterion mandates "systematic observation, measurement and experiment".

During cross-examination and re-examination at trial, a striking evidentiary gap emerged regarding how JTR conducted its physical trials: rather than testing an actual curtain, the team hoisted a weight of approximately 800 pounds, "guesstimated" to match the Ryerson University curtain (believed to weigh 800 to 1,000 pounds), without knowing the exact weight used, and Mr. Marineau testified that they had no way of measuring, and took no measurements of, how fast the weight fell; there was no indication that a stopwatch or even the second hand of a wristwatch was used to compare descents against the 30-second objective. Justice Sommerfeldt's comment on this omission is central to his analysis of the scientific method, observing that if the scientific method had been used—meaning systematic observation, measurement, and experiment—Mr. Marineau and his colleagues would have determined the precise weight used in the experiments and would have precisely measured the duration of the descent in each experiment so that they could determine whether, as they moved from one experiment to the next, the duration of the descent was increasing or decreasing.

This passage illustrates an important practical boundary, although Justice Sommerfeldt expressly noted that he was not aware of any jurisprudence establishing that trial and error does not come within the scientific method, while observing that several cases suggest it may well fall outside it; in his analysis, the distinction between a systematic scientific investigation and "trial and error" turned on measurement and the systematic comparison of results. In applied mechanics, velocity is a function of distance over time (v = d/t), and gravitational force is a direct function of mass (F = mg). When attempting to control the rate of descent of a gravity-driven curtain, curtain mass and descent duration are the two most fundamental physical parameters in the system. By failing to determine the exact test weight and failing to measure the exact duration of the descent in each trial, JTR had no objective metric to evaluate whether an engineering modification improved or degraded system performance. Relying on subjective visual observation (watching the test weight fall "with the naked eye", in the Court's words) reduces product development to intuitive tinkering.
Evidentiary Deficiencies: Contemporaneous Documentation, Oral Testimony, and Consultant Reliance

The fourth cluster of failures involves JTR's evidentiary presentation, specifically the complete absence of contemporaneous test records and the reliance on retrospective reconstructions prepared by an external tax consultant.

In Canadian tax law, as noted by Justice Archambault in 116736 Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 1998 CanLII 398 (TCC), and reaffirmed in Canafric Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 108, the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations do not contain an explicit statutory requirement that written technical reports be produced as a condition precedent to claiming SR&ED expenditures; in principle, a taxpayer may adduce evidence by way of credible oral testimony to fill gaps in documentary records. Similarly, as confirmed in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King, 2024 TCC 159, contemporaneous documentation does not need to be formatted like a peer-reviewed academic paper designed for an outsider unfamiliar with the field to replicate results, provided it keeps track of the hypotheses generated, experiments undertaken, and results obtained.

However, JTR demonstrates the fatal limits of relying on oral testimony when contemporaneous empirical data was never generated in the first place. Unlike in Canafric or Manning Canning, where witnesses provided detailed, factually grounded testimony supported by progressive batch or formulation records showing why failed iterations were adjusted, Mr. Marineau could not testify to the exact test weight or the measured descent durations because those measurements were never taken during the Fire Curtain Project (June 2007 to April 2008, in JTR's 2008 taxation year); moreover, JTR discarded the plans for designs that did not work and kept no record of changes in variables and results. As the Court emphasized, relying on RIS-Christie, the only sure-fire way of establishing that research was undertaken systematically is documentary evidence revealing the logical progression between each test and preceding or subsequent tests, and JTR's failure to adduce any notes, sketches, drawings or other documents made during its experiments hampered its ability to show a systematic investigation.

Furthermore, Justice Sommerfeldt scrutinized the role of the external consultant whose firm prepared JTR's Form T661 claims. While the preparer's witness, Mr. Todd Louie (an accountant and Director of Taxation at Sheldon & Milstein Tax Consultants Ltd.), had experience preparing and overseeing SR&ED expenditure claims (Form T661) for various clients, he had no formal training in mechanical engineering and no university degree in engineering, and he did not work on or observe any of JTR's experiments; the PhDs and engineers he said Sheldon employed did not testify. In JTR, the Experiment Summary Sheets prepared by Sheldon after the experiments were completed could not show a contemporaneous logical progression of tests, and Mr. Louie's view that four patents represented the routine engineering available at the time was not accepted because he was not qualified as an expert; if the underlying technical personnel did not conduct systematic, measured experiments contemporaneously, a consultant's polished Form T661 prose cannot retroactively manufacture scientific eligibility.
Inability to Substantiate Technological Advancement and Commercial Boundaries

Finally, on the fourth Northwest Hydraulic criterion (technological advancement), the Court found that it had no reliable evidence of the general understanding of persons knowledgeable in mechanical engineering in 2007 through 2009 because no scientists or engineers testified; it held that JTR's description of the Fire Curtain Project did not describe a technological advancement and that the Manual Override description read more as a statement of objectives, noting that novelty or innovation alone is not sufficient.

In SR&ED jurisprudence, a commercial or functional advancement (creating a marketable rigging product that works for 95% of theatre curtains) is legally distinct from a technological advancement (generating new scientific or engineering knowledge that advances the understanding of applied mechanics for competent professionals in the field). Although JTR successfully fabricated a functional descent-control device, it generated no quantifiable engineering data—such as validated mathematical models relating curtain mass, braking torque, and descent velocity—that added to the technological knowledge base. Moreover, JTR did not disprove the Minister's assumption that the claimed 2008 activities were limited to the design, purchasing, adjustments, arrangements, pump selection and valve changes relating to three customer contracts (Ryerson University, the Richmond Hill Theatre and the Persephone Theatre), although the decision did not rest on the statutory exclusion for commercial production under subsection 248(1).
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and jurisprudential requirement examined in Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen against the taxpayer's specific legal and evidentiary failures and the corresponding standard of proof enforced by the Tax Court of Canada.

headers: Taxpayer's Specific Failure in Joel Theatrical Rigging (2017 TCC 6)
Tax Court of Canada's Standard of Proof

cells: 1. Technological Risk or Uncertainty (Existence of a technical problem unresolvable by routine engineering or standard procedures)
Income Tax Act, s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC) (Criterion 1)

JTR presented a practical product design goal (controlling the rate of descent of fire curtains with a motor, hydraulic pump and valves, without counterweights, within the 30-second fire code limit) as a technological uncertainty. No scientist or engineer testified as to the techniques, procedures and data generally accessible to mechanical engineers in 2008 and 2009, and four patents produced by an accountant not qualified as an expert did not establish the state of available technology; the Manual Override Project's uncertainty was not clearly articulated and its work was found to be routine engineering. Justice Sommerfeldt noted the Fire Curtain Project "may well have been routine engineering".

The taxpayer must prove on a balance of probabilities that competent professionals in the field could not resolve the problem using publicly available knowledge, standard engineering calculations, or routine component tuning. If known solutions are used, the taxpayer must prove "system uncertainty" arising from their novel integration.
2. Formulation of Specific Hypotheses (Formulating causal statements aimed at reducing or eliminating the technological uncertainty)
Income Tax Act, s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 2); Advanced Agricultural Testing Inc. v. The Queen, 2009 TCC 190

The purported hypotheses in the Experiment Summary Sheets (prepared by Sheldon after the experiments) appeared only as "next steps" entries, were not formulated as propositions to be tested, and were missing for several experiments. Although a Part 2 statement in the 2008 claim may have been a hypothesis and the Part 2 hypotheses in the 2009 claim were adequately formulated, the steps they contemplated appeared to be routine engineering.

As defined by Justice Sommerfeldt at para 26, "a hypothesis is a statement to be tested by an experiment or a trial". The taxpayer must establish that specific, causal hypotheses preceded each experimental iteration rather than relying on a single overarching product objective.
3. Systematic Investigation (Scientific Method) (Procedures according with systematic observation, measurement, and experiment)
Income Tax Act, s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 3); RIS-Christie Ltd. v. Canada, 1998 CanLII 8876 (FCA)

JTR failed to measure fundamental physical variables during its trials. Specifically, Mr. Marineau and his team did not know the exact weight of the approximately 800-pound test weight used in the experiments and did not measure the duration of its descent across sequential trials; the Manual Override reconfigurations involved no measurement, and the Court questioned whether trained observation occurred, as no team member held an engineering degree or P.Eng. designation. They relied on subjective visual assessment ("trial and error").

The taxpayer must demonstrate systematic observation, quantitative measurement, and controlled experimentation. Key independent variables (e.g., exact mass) and dependent variables (e.g., exact descent duration) must be precisely measured from trial to trial to objectively determine whether performance is increasing or decreasing.
4. Technological Advancement (Generation of new scientific or technological knowledge)
Income Tax Act, s. 248(1)(c); Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 4); Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 TCC 261, aff’d 2011 FCA 355

JTR's claim described its objective of developing universal technology for hydraulically controlled backwinding systems for fire curtains, which the Court found did not describe a technological advancement. Because no scientists or engineers testified, the Court had no reliable evidence of the general understanding of persons knowledgeable in mechanical engineering in 2007 through 2009, and the Manual Override description read more as a statement of objectives; novelty or innovation alone was not sufficient.

The taxpayer must distinguish product functionality from technological advancement. The process must generate new technological information or advance the general engineering understanding of competent professionals in the relevant field, even if the advancement is incremental.
5. Contemporaneous Documentation (Maintaining detailed records of hypotheses tested and results as work progresses)
Northwest Hydraulic (Criterion 5); CW Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393; 116736 Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 1998 CanLII 398 (TCC)

JTR kept no notes, sketches, drawings or records of changes in variables and results, and discarded the plans for designs that did not work. Oral testimony at trial could not cure the absence of records because the underlying empirical measurements were never taken. The Experiment Summary Sheets were prepared by the external advisor after the experiments were completed, and the advisor's witness, an accountant, was not qualified as an expert, which hampered JTR's ability to show a systematic investigation.

While written reports are not an absolute statutory mandate under s. 248(1) if credible oral testimony fills the gaps, the taxpayer must present reliable evidence—ideally contemporaneous test logs—recording the exact parameters, hypotheses tested, quantitative results, and iterative design modifications to prove the work was not random trial-and-error.
6. Separation of SR&ED from Commercial Production & Filing Compliance (Demarcation of eligible expenditures and prescribed Form T661 filing)
Income Tax Act, ss. 37(1), 127(5), 127(9)(m), 248(1); Easy Way Cattle Oilers Ltd. v. The Queen, 2016 FCA 301

JTR did not disprove the Minister's assumption that the claimed 2008 activities were limited to design, purchasing, adjustments, arrangements, pump selection and valve changes relating to three customer contracts and constituted routine work; filing compliance was not at issue in the decision.

The taxpayer must clearly track and segregate eligible experimental hours and materials from ineligible commercial production and routine engineering within the taxation year, and must file prescribed Form T661 (and, to claim ITCs, the prescribed Schedule 31 under paragraph 127(9)(m), as confirmed in Easy Way Cattle Oilers) containing complete prescribed technical and financial information within 12 months of the corporate filing due date.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the legal holdings of Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen into actionable compliance protocols for Canadian taxpayers, the following two applied industry case studies examine realistic technical projects that exhibit the exact vulnerabilities identified by Justice Sommerfeldt. Each case study provides a comprehensive, step-by-step remedial restructuring across project governance, baseline technical documentation, commercial and consultant contract architecture, and quantitative experimentation tracking to satisfy subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act and the Northwest Hydraulic five-question test.
Case Study 1: Applied Mechanical and Mechatronic Rigging (Acoustic Arena Hoist and Passive Eddy-Current Braking System)
Industry Scenario and Vulnerability Profile

StageTech Kinetic Systems Inc. ("StageTech") is a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) based in Vaughan, Ontario, that designs and manufactures custom overhead rigging hoists and acoustic baffle deployment systems for multipurpose arenas and performing arts centres across Canada. StageTech is contracted by a municipal performing arts centre to design and install a rapid-deployment overhead acoustic canopy and emergency safety drop system. Due to strict structural roof-load limits in the heritage venue, StageTech cannot use conventional heavy cast-iron counterweights or heavy hydraulic braking manifolds. Instead, StageTech attempts to develop an ultra-lightweight, passive magnetic (eddy-current) rotary braking drum integrated directly into a high-ratio planetary cable hoist. The technical goal is to allow a 1,200 kg acoustic array to descend under gravity during a power failure at a strictly controlled velocity of 0.45 m/s ± 0.05 m/s and decelerate to a soft stop within the final 1.2 m of travel without external electrical power.

Left to its traditional shop-floor habits, StageTech's fabrication lead and two millwrights build three prototype aluminum rotor drums, swap out different arrangements of neodymium magnets on the stator, and drop a test load in their warehouse. They do not calculate the theoretical Lorentz braking torque limits beforehand, do not weigh the ballast blocks precisely, and judge the descent speed visually as "too fast," "too jerky," or "just right". At year-end, StageTech hires a contingency-fee SR&ED preparer with an accounting background who drafts a generic Form T661 claiming 1,800 shop-floor hours, including the time spent fabricating the final commercial hoist installed at the client's venue. Applying the reasoning in Joel Theatrical Rigging, the CRA would likely disallow 100% of this claim on the grounds of routine engineering, lack of formulated hypotheses, absence of quantitative measurement, and unsegregated commercial production.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance and Technical Oversight

In JTR, the Tax Court noted that no professional engineer was on the team or consulted during the experiments and that none of JTR's designers held an engineering degree or P.Eng. designation, and accordingly questioned whether trained observation occurred. To remedy this governance deficiency prior to commencing physical shop-floor work, StageTech must establish an internal SR&ED Project Review Committee under the direction of a qualified technical lead. Specifically, StageTech designates its Senior Mechanical Engineer (P.Eng., licensed with Professional Engineers Ontario) as the Principal Investigator. While shop-floor millwrights and Canadian Welding Bureau (CWB) certified welders execute the physical prototype modifications, the P.Eng. authors the experimental protocol, defines the physical variables to be measured, and signs off on each experimental iteration.

Concurrently, StageTech's governance protocols must formally separate the lifecycle of the project into three distinct cost centres within its enterprise resource planning (ERP) time-tracking system to address the CRA's standard objection that the nature and extent of eligible work conducted in the tax period is unclear. Phase A captures ineligible pre-SR&ED baseline activities, such as standard structural load calculations, computer-aided design (CAD) drafting of known hoist housings, and vendor component sourcing. Phase B isolates eligible SR&ED experimental development, encompassing iterative design, numerical simulation, bench-scale testing, and full-scale rig testing specifically dedicated to resolving the thermo-magnetic eddy-current braking decay uncertainty. Finally, Phase C segregates ineligible commercial production and installation activities, ensuring that final fabrication of the venue-specific hoist once the rotor and stator geometry is frozen, CWB production welding, Technical Standards and Safety Authority (TSSA) safety certification, and on-site arena installation are excluded from the Form T661 expenditure pool.
Step 2: Establishing the Technical Baseline and Technological Uncertainty Documentation

To defeat the "routine engineering" objection that proved fatal in JTR, StageTech must produce a formal, dated Technological Baseline and Uncertainty Brief before building the first physical prototype. As highlighted in Canadian SR&ED commentary, the purpose of baseline documentation is to establish the existing industry benchmark or knowledge base and substantiate how the company's activities seek to advance beyond that benchmark through literature reviews, background research, and engineering calculations. In this dossier, StageTech's P.Eng. documents that standard passive eddy-current brakes rely on thick copper or aluminum discs rotating through a static magnetic field. However, standard electromagnetic braking equations demonstrate that as kinetic energy converts into thermal energy inside a compact hoist drum during a continuous 25 m gravitational drop, the electrical conductivity (σ) of the aluminum rotor drops rapidly due to Joule heating, causing "thermal brake fade" and runaway acceleration.

Building on this baseline calculation, StageTech documents why routine engineering cannot resolve the problem, establishing classic "system uncertainty". Specifically, increasing the permanent magnet flux density to compensate for thermal fade causes excessive starting drag at low rotational speeds, which prevents the canopy or curtain from initiating descent under lighter load configurations; conversely, adding external cooling fins increases rotational inertia and violates the venue's strict 85 kg hoist mass ceiling. Consequently, StageTech defines its Technological Uncertainty with mathematical precision: whether a passive, variable-air-gap cam-actuated Halbach magnet array can dynamically modulate magnetic flux density inversely to rotor temperature rise during a continuous 25 m gravitational drop to maintain a linear descent velocity of 0.45 m/s ± 0.05 m/s without exceeding a rotor surface temperature of 160°C or an overall assembly mass of 85 kg.
Step 3: Restructuring Commercial and Consultant Contract Terms

To prevent statutory disqualification under the contract payment and funded research rules of subsections 37(1) and 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, and to avoid the evidentiary trap of relying on an unqualified T661 preparer as seen in JTR, StageTech must execute two critical contractual restructurings. First, regarding the municipal arena contract, if a client pays StageTech to perform engineering R&D on its behalf, those receipts constitute a "contract payment" under subsection 127(9), reducing StageTech's qualified SR&ED expenditures dollar-for-dollar. StageTech must therefore structure its commercial agreement with the venue strictly as a Fixed-Price Deliverable Contract for Commercial Goods Installation—supplying a physical acoustic hoist meeting specified performance parameters—rather than a service contract for engineering development. The contract must incorporate an explicit Intellectual Property and Financial Risk Clause stipulating that StageTech retains 100% legal and beneficial ownership of all background and foreground intellectual property, patents, CAD designs, and experimental data relating to the passive eddy-current braking mechanism, that StageTech bears the sole financial risk of engineering failure or prototype cost overruns, and that the venue pays only for the final physical hoist hardware upon successful commercial acceptance testing.

Second, StageTech must overhaul its external SR&ED advisor engagement contract. In JTR, Justice Sommerfeldt noted that although the external claim preparer had filed Form T661 claims for various clients, he lacked technical qualifications in the relevant engineering field. StageTech's consulting agreement must mandate that the advisory firm assigns a qualified Mechanical Engineer (P.Eng.) to conduct quarterly contemporaneous technical interviews with StageTech's Principal Investigator. Rather than drafting retrospective narratives after year-end, the consultant's contractual scope is restricted to compiling and indexing StageTech's contemporaneous test logs into the prescribed Form T661 format, with all Form T661 Part 2 technical narratives reviewed, verified, and signed off by StageTech's internal P.Eng. well in advance of the 12-month statutory filing deadline under subsection 37(11).
Step 4: Implementing Quantitative Experimentation Tracking and Hypothesis Logs

Directly addressing Justice Sommerfeldt's central critique in JTR—that Mr. Marineau and his colleagues neither determined the precise weight used in the experiments nor precisely measured the duration of the descent across sequential trials—StageTech instruments its warehouse test rig with calibrated metrology equipment. This instrumentation includes a digital crane load cell measuring payload mass to ±0.1 kg, a laser rotary optical encoder mounted on the hoist drum measuring instantaneous velocity, acceleration, and total descent duration to ±0.01 seconds, and an infrared pyrometer recording rotor surface temperature in degrees Celsius. Every physical trial is recorded contemporaneously in a structured SR&ED Hypothesis and Empirical Trial Ledger, as detailed in the table below.

Case Study 2: Custom Food Processing and Fluid-Thermal Engineering (Continuous-Flow Shear-Sensitive Antimicrobial Dosing System)
Industry Scenario and Vulnerability Profile

Boreal NutriProcess Corp. ("Boreal") is a food and beverage processing and equipment engineering company located in Laval, Quebec, that develops shelf-stable, functional plant-based and fermented vinegar-botanical beverages for retail distribution across Canada. Boreal seeks to eliminate thermal pasteurization—which destroys heat-sensitive probiotic metabolites and volatile flavour compounds—in its high-viscosity fermented oat-vinegar beverage while achieving 12-month ambient shelf stability at room temperature (22°C). Standard chemical preservatives known to competent professionals in the field, specifically potassium sorbate and sodium benzoate, flocculate and precipitate out of solution when injected into Boreal's high-pectin, low-pH (3.6) matrix, whereas natural mushroom-derived chitosan preservative ("Chiber") causes severe non-Newtonian shear-thickening inside Boreal's continuous-flow inline cavitation mixer, seizing the metering pumps. Boreal attempts to engineer a modified ultrasonic-assisted micro-dosing manifold and buffer stabilization protocol to disperse the natural antimicrobial uniformly without triggering hydrocolloid gelation.

In a typical non-compliant workflow, Boreal's production supervisor and quality technician run 15 pilot batches on the factory floor over four months, tweaking pump speeds and preservative ratios by hand. When a batch thickens or spoils during shelf-life holding, they simply discard the recipe without analyzing the underlying rheological or microbial failure mechanism, and without measuring inline shear rates, droplet micron sizes, or exact microbial log-reduction kinetics. When audited by the CRA, Boreal presents only final commercial recipes and purchase invoices for raw ingredients. Under Joel Theatrical Rigging—and contrasting against successful taxpayer outcomes in Canafric Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 108, and Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King, 2024 TCC 159—Boreal's claim would be disallowed unless it bridges the evidentiary chasm between unrecorded kitchen trial-and-error and a documented, hypothesis-driven systematic investigation.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance and Technical Oversight

To satisfy the Tax Court's expectation that SR&ED is directed by competent professionals applying the scientific method, Boreal institutes cross-disciplinary technical supervision prior to initiating pilot trials. Boreal assigns its Director of Food Science (holding an M.Sc. in Food Microbiology) and its Process Automation Engineer (Ing., licensed with the Ordre des ingénieurs du Québec) to co-direct the experimental program.

Drawing directly on the judicial distinction highlighted in Canafric Inc. and Joel Theatrical Rigging, Boreal implements a mandatory governance protocol governing failed recipe and process trials: no unsuccessful formulation or pilot run may be discarded without a documented root-cause analysis. In Canafric, the Tax Court ruled in favour of the taxpayer precisely because the company did not merely dismiss unsuccessful recipes, but systematically analyzed why each failed recipe did not meet technical requirements and adjusted the formulation accordingly. Under Boreal's restructured governance, every failed pilot run must undergo quantitative rheological viscometry and microbial challenge plating to determine why the tested hypothesis failed before the next formulation or manifold nozzle geometry is authorized.
Step 2: Establishing the Technical Baseline and Technological Uncertainty Documentation

In Manning Canning Kitchens, the Tax Court held that testing Chiber (a white button mushroom extract previously used only in dairy products) in a vinegar-based, cold-pressed juice beverage was not routine engineering, even though the Minister argued that preservatives such as potassium sorbate and sodium benzoate were known to competent professionals in the field; a known ingredient can thus give rise to technological uncertainty where it has never been applied in the specific technical context and routine procedures cannot remove the uncertainty. Conversely, in JTR, the taxpayer failed to prove why standard procedures were inadequate. Boreal therefore establishes its technical baseline in a formal Technical Feasibility and Literature Benchmark Dossier prior to pilot testing.

In this baseline dossier, Boreal compiles vendor technical data sheets for potassium sorbate, sodium benzoate, and Chiber (0.05%–0.15% w/w), alongside standard inline static mixing equations. Boreal records preliminary bench tests proving that standard dosing of potassium sorbate and sodium benzoate at pH 3.6 in a 4.2% β-glucan oat matrix induces electrostatic bridging and sedimentation within 48 hours, whereas substituting Chiber increases dynamic viscosity (μ) from 180 cP to over 2,400 cP under standard pump shear (> 1,500 s⁻¹). Having demonstrated the failure of standard procedures, Boreal defines its exact Technological Uncertainty: whether acoustic cavitation dispersion at 20–40 kHz coupled with divalent cation chelation can suppress polycationic cross-linking between Chiber (chitosan polymer) and negatively charged oat β-glucan chains during continuous inline injection, achieving a greater than 5-log reduction in acid-tolerant spoilage yeast (Zygosaccharomyces bailii) over 12 months at 22°C while maintaining dynamic viscosity below 250 cP.
Step 3: Restructuring Commercial and Consultant Contract Terms

Because food and beverage processors frequently develop custom formulations alongside retail grocery chains, Boreal must insulate its SR&ED expenditure pool from commercial contract exclusions under subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act. To prevent retail partner milestone payments from being classified as "contract payments"—and to prevent the project from being characterized as routine commercial recipe customization—Boreal separates its commercial supply agreements from its internal R&D governance. Any product development fee charged to a retail client is structured strictly as a commercial slotting or packaging deposit refundable against future commercial unit volume purchases, while the master supply agreement explicitly stipulates that Boreal conducts all shelf-life preservation and ultrasonic processing engineering on its own account, bears the sole financial risk of failed pilot batches, and retains exclusive ownership of all process patents, manifold designs, and trade secrets.

Simultaneously, where Boreal engages third-party Canadian laboratories for specialized microbial challenge testing or laser diffraction particle sizing, the subcontracts are drafted as Eligible Third-Party SR&ED Performer Contracts pursuant to subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) and subsection 127(9) of the Act. Each subcontract explicitly states that the Canadian laboratory is performing analytical support work (microbial plating and rheological profiling) commensurate with the needs of, and directly in support of, Boreal's core experimental development under paragraph 248(1)(d) of the Act, with all raw quantitative data delivered directly into Boreal's contemporaneous experimental repository.
Step 4: Implementing Quantitative Experimentation Tracking and Hypothesis Logs

To ensure that Boreal's documentation satisfies both Joel Theatrical Rigging (precise measurement of inputs and outputs across sequential experiments to determine whether target metrics are increasing or decreasing) and Manning Canning Kitchens (contemporaneous records tracking hypotheses generated, experiments undertaken, and results obtained), Boreal establishes a digital Pilot Trial and Rheological/Microbial Measurement Log, as structured in the table below.

body.text: Synthesis of Legal and Technical Takeaways for Canadian Practitioners

The Tax Court of Canada's decision in Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen serves as an enduring cautionary benchmark in Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence. Even when a Canadian manufacturer, processor, or engineering contractor encounters a genuine operational challenge and successfully invents a commercially effective mechanical device or process—such as JTR's fire curtain descent-control system—the claim will fail at the Tax Court if the taxpayer cannot prove how and why the development transcended routine engineering through a hypothesis-driven, quantitatively measured experimental process. By embedding formal technical governance, documenting the failure of standard engineering procedures at the outset, insulating commercial contracts from funded-research exclusions, and systematically measuring and recording exact physical parameters across every experimental iteration, Canadian taxpayers can build an audit-proof evidentiary record that satisfies both the Canada Revenue Agency and the Tax Court of Canada.
